models.model_label: OLS time-trend regression for propensity to avoid quarterly losses
models.sample_description: One annual standardized-difference statistic per calendar year, 1985–2002 (18 regression observations), for the avoid quarterly losses threshold. The yearly statistics are calculated from the main firm-quarter data, using the bin immediately left of zero and a common standardized sample size of 1,000. The underlying main-analysis firm-quarter sample totals 111,485 observations over 1985–2002; those firm-quarter counts are not the N for this time-trend regression.

dependent_variable.name: Standardized difference: avoid quarterly losses
dependent_variable.definition: Burgstahler–Dichev standardized difference for the avoid-loss threshold (quarterly earnings level deflated by beginning-of-quarter-t stock price) in year y, evaluated in the earnings bin just left of zero. It is the actual observation count minus the expected count, divided by the estimated standard deviation of that difference; the expected count is the average of the two adjacent bins. The authors compute the threshold-year statistic using a standardized N of 1,000 based on the actual bin proportion. Bins have width .0025. A negative value indicates threshold achievement; |statistic| ≥ 2.33 is the stated one-tailed threshold criterion.
dependent_variable.formula: SDiff_avoid-loss,y = (Observed_left_bin_y − Expected_left_bin_y) / EstimatedSD(Observed − Expected); Expected_left_bin_y = mean(counts in adjacent bins); counts rescaled to N=1,000.

sample_extraction.data_section_full_text:
Sample Selection

We obtain actual quarterly earnings, analyst forecasts of quarterly earnings, stock prices,
and earnings announcement dates from Thomson Financial I/B/E/S for 19 years, 1984–
2002. We require earnings lagged by four quarters to measure our second threshold, earnings changes, so our study period is 18 years, 1985–2002. We calculate three-day marketadjusted cumulative abnormal returns around quarterly earnings announcements and obtain
SIC codes using CRSP data.

We use the single most recent forecast made by the timeliest analyst(s) prior to the
earnings announcement date as our analyst forecast. <sup>8</sup> We define earnings changes as reported earnings in quarter t minus those in quarter t �4, and earnings surprises as reported
earnings in quarter t minus the analyst’s forecast of earnings in quarter t . We deflate earnings
levels, earnings changes and earnings surprises by beginning of quarter t stock price. <sup>9</sup> All
firm-quarter observations require reported earnings in both quarter t and quarter t �4, an
analyst forecast of quarter t earnings, stock price at the beginning of quarter t, and returns
data for the three days, �1 to �1, where day 0 is the earnings announcement day.

Consistent with Burgstahler and Dichev (1997), we delete firms with SIC codes 4400–
5000 (regulated industries) and 6000–6500 (financial institutions). To calculate analyst forecast dispersion, we take the standard deviation of analyst forecasts prior to the earnings
announcement date, deflated by stock price (Kinney et al. 2002). For this analysis, we
require firms to be followed by at least three analysts. To remove the effects of outliers,
we delete three-day market-adjusted cumulative abnormal returns in the two extreme percentiles. <sup>10</sup> Our sample for the main analysis consists of 111,485 firm-quarter observations.
